claim: Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops are largely conceived as parallel circuits that process limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information separately.
source: Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops are largely conceived as parallel circuits that process limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information separately.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing conceptualization in the field, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: A unidirectional influence of the limbic over the motor loop exists via ventral striatum-substantia nigra (SNr)-motor thalamus circuitry.
source: Despite largely closed loops within each functional domain, we discovered a unidirectional influence of the limbic over the motor loop via ventral striatum-substantia nigra (SNr)-motor thalamus circuitry.
evidence: This claim is supported by the systematic mapping experiments described in the manuscript using genetic and viral approaches.

claim: The projection from ventral striatum functionally inhibits nigro-thalamic SNr neurons.
source: Slice electrophysiology verifies that the projection from ventral striatum functionally inhibits nigro-thalamic SNr neurons.
evidence: This is directly supported by ex vivo electrophysiology experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ventral striatum to SNr pathway modulates activity in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: In vivo optogenetic stimulation of ventral or dorsolateral striatum to SNr pathway modulates activity in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and motor cortex (M1), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo optogenetic experiments with electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of dorsolateral striatum to SNr pathway modulates activity in motor cortex (M1).
source: In vivo optogenetic stimulation of ventral or dorsolateral striatum to SNr pathway modulates activity in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and motor cortex (M1), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo optogenetic experiments with electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The dorsolateral striatum-SNr pathway exerts little impact on mPFC.
source: However, whereas the dorsolateral striatum-SNr pathway exerts little impact on mPFC, activation of the ventral striatum-SNr pathway effectively alters M1 activity.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing minimal responses in mPFC to DLS stimulation.

claim: Activation of the ventral striatum-SNr pathway effectively alters M1 activity.
source: However, whereas the dorsolateral striatum-SNr pathway exerts little impact on mPFC, activation of the ventral striatum-SNr pathway effectively alters M1 activity.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing significant M1 responses to VS stimulation.

claim: Limbic information can modulate motor output through ventral striatum control of M1.
source: These results demonstrate an open cortico-basal ganglia loop whereby limbic information could modulate motor output through ventral striatum control of M1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined anatomical and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cortico-basal ganglia circuits are crucial for emotional, cognitive, and sensorimotor functions in health and disease.
source: Cortico-basal ganglia circuits are crucial for emotional, cognitive, and sensorimotor functions in health and disease (Doya, 2000; Floresco, 2015; Gerdeman et al., 2003; Graybiel et al., 1994; Gunaydin and Kreitzer, 2016; Hikosaka et al., 2000; Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Jin and Costa, 2015; Marchand, 2010; Vaghi et al., 2017; Yin and Knowlton, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Virtually all cortical regions project to the striatum.
source: Virtually all cortical regions project to the striatum, the main input nucleus of the basal ganglia, which plays an important role in guiding behavior (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Hooks et al., 2018; Voorn et al., 2004; Witten et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2009; Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The striatum is the main input nucleus of the basal ganglia.
source: Virtually all cortical regions project to the striatum, the main input nucleus of the basal ganglia, which plays an important role in guiding behavior (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Hooks et al., 2018; Voorn et al., 2004; Witten et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2009; Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of basal ganglia anatomy.

claim: The striatum plays an important role in guiding behavior.
source: Virtually all cortical regions project to the striatum, the main input nucleus of the basal ganglia, which plays an important role in guiding behavior (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Hooks et al., 2018; Voorn et al., 2004; Witten et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2009; Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The 'sensorimotor' dorsolateral striatum (DLS) receives inputs from motor cortex.
source: For example, the 'sensorimotor' dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which receives inputs from motor cortex, plays a role in executing body movements (Barbera et al., 2016; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Yin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The dorsolateral striatum (DLS) plays a role in executing body movements.
source: For example, the 'sensorimotor' dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which receives inputs from motor cortex, plays a role in executing body movements (Barbera et al., 2016; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Yin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The 'limbic' ventral striatum (VS) receives limbic but not motor cortical input.
source: However, the 'limbic' ventral striatum (VS), which receives limbic but not motor cortical input, also alters behavioral output including locomotion activity, approach/avoidance behaviors, and recovery of skilled movement after spinal cord injury (Britt et al., 2012; Floresco, 2015; Saunders and Robinson, 2012; Sawada et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ventral striatum (VS) alters behavioral output including locomotion activity, approach/avoidance behaviors, and recovery of skilled movement after spinal cord injury.
source: However, the 'limbic' ventral striatum (VS), which receives limbic but not motor cortical input, also alters behavioral output including locomotion activity, approach/avoidance behaviors, and recovery of skilled movement after spinal cord injury (Britt et al., 2012; Floresco, 2015; Saunders and Robinson, 2012; Sawada et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For a unified behavioral output, information across different modalities must be integrated into motor circuits to drive action appropriately.
source: These findings suggest that for a unified behavioral output, information across the different modalities must be integrated into motor circuits to drive action appropriately (Mogenson et al., 1980).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and the observations about VS function.

claim: Some studies have implicated mechanisms for limbic-motor interactions in the dopaminergic system.
source: Though some studies have implicated mechanisms for limbic-motor interactions in the dopaminergic system (Beier et al., 2015; Belin and Everitt, 2008; Haber et al., 2000; Lerner et al., 2015; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2018), how limbic information ultimately reaches motor circuitry remains largely unknown, as do the characteristics of its influence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: How limbic information ultimately reaches motor circuitry remains largely unknown.
source: Though some studies have implicated mechanisms for limbic-motor interactions in the dopaminergic system (Beier et al., 2015; Belin and Everitt, 2008; Haber et al., 2000; Lerner et al., 2015; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2018), how limbic information ultimately reaches motor circuitry remains largely unknown, as do the characteristics of its influence.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops have been largely conceptualized as closed, functionally segregated loops, in which limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information are processed in parallel.
source: Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops have been largely conceptualized as closed, functionally segregated loops, in which limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information are processed in parallel (Alexander et al., 1986; Deniau et al., 1996; Haber, 2003; Kim and Hikosaka, 2015; Montaron et al., 1996; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the prevailing model.

claim: Older studies proposed a 'funnel-like' architecture for basal ganglia output, such that each loop provides some input to the motor circuit.
source: Alternatively, older studies proposed a 'funnel-like' architecture for basal ganglia output, such that each loop provides some input to the motor circuit (Allen and Tsukahara, 1974; Kemp and Powell, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to older literature proposing an alternative model.

claim: A 'partially-open' loop architecture in the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry has been suggested from primate studies.
source: A 'partially-open' loop architecture in the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry has been suggested from primate studies (Joel and Weiner, 1994; Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006), but this previous evidence is incomplete and the precise anatomical basis underlying connections between functionally distinct loops has not been identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to primate studies.

claim: Previous evidence for partially-open loop architecture is incomplete and the precise anatomical basis underlying connections between functionally distinct loops has not been identified.
source: A 'partially-open' loop architecture in the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry has been suggested from primate studies (Joel and Weiner, 1994; Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006), but this previous evidence is incomplete and the precise anatomical basis underlying connections between functionally distinct loops has not been identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior work, identifying a gap in knowledge.

claim: Studies have largely focused on mapping monosynaptic inputs from cortex to the striatum, emphasizing the topographic organization at the level of cortico-striatal projections.
source: As a result, studies have largely focused on mapping monosynaptic inputs from cortex to the striatum (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Hooks et al., 2018; Voorn et al., 2004), emphasizing the topographic organization at the level of cortico-striatal projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is incompletely understood how distinct 'channels' proceed through the rest of basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry and whether they interact at all.
source: To date, it is incompletely understood how these distinct 'channels' proceed through the rest of basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuitry and whether they interact at all.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The limbic and motor loops provide a model to investigate how distinct cortico-basal ganglia loops are organized throughout basal ganglia output.
source: In the current study, we focused on limbic and motor cortico-basal ganglia loops that originate from the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and primary motor cortex (M1). These limbic and motor loops provide a model to investigate how distinct cortico-basal ganglia loops are organized throughout basal ganglia output, which we mapped using multiple genetic and viral tracing tools.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale and approach of the current study.

claim: A novel one-way interaction across cortico-basal ganglia loops exists, in which the limbic loop exerts a unidirectional influence over the motor loop that is mediated by ventral striatum-medial SNr-motor thalamus circuitry.
source: In addition to the closed loop within each functional domain, we identified a novel one-way interaction across these cortico-basal ganglia loops, in which the limbic loop exerts a unidirectional influence over the motor loop that is mediated by ventral striatum-medial SNr-motor thalamus circuitry.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by anatomical tracing data.

claim: VS functionally inhibits medial SNr neurons that project to motor thalamus.
source: Using slice physiology and optogenetics, we show that VS functionally inhibits medial SNr neurons that project to motor thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Optogenetic activation of VS terminals in the SNr results in significant activation of M1.
source: Consistent with our anatomical findings, the in vivo recording experiments showed, in addition to the within-loop activation in which VS activated mPFC and DLS activated M1, significant activation of M1 when VS terminals in the SNr were stimulated.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: DLS output does not effectively modulate activity in mPFC.
source: Conversely, DLS output did not effectively modulate activity in mPFC.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology experiments showing minimal mPFC responses to DLS stimulation.

claim: An open cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop exists through which VS can modulate M1 activity.
source: Together, these results demonstrate an open cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop through which VS can modulate M1 activity, providing new insights into the limbic control over motor output in health and disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: 66–70 hr is adequate survival time for 3rd-order infection of Wt-RABV without 4th-order infection in rats.
source: Prior studies have established that 66–70 hr is adequate survival time for 3rd-order infection of Wt-RABV without 4th-order infection in rats (Aoki et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2012), so this procedure could determine tri-synaptic connections originating from striatum to cortex via the direct pathway (Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior methodological studies.

claim: The M1 injection revealed CTb+ terminals that overlapped with Wt-RABV+ neurons in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS).
source: The M1 injection revealed CTb+ terminals that overlapped with Wt-RABV+ neurons in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which is known to process motor information (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Voorn et al., 2004), thus providing evidence for a closed motor loop between M1 and DLS.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments.

claim: The DLS is known to process motor information.
source: The M1 injection revealed CTb+ terminals that overlapped with Wt-RABV+ neurons in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which is known to process motor information (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Voorn et al., 2004), thus providing evidence for a closed motor loop between M1 and DLS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is a closed motor loop between M1 and DLS.
source: The M1 injection revealed CTb+ terminals that overlapped with Wt-RABV+ neurons in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS), which is known to process motor information (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Voorn et al., 2004), thus providing evidence for a closed motor loop between M1 and DLS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical tracing data showing overlap of inputs and outputs.

claim: M1 injections labeled a large number of Wt-RABV+ neurons outside the CTb-labeled zone in DLS, including the dorsomedial (DMS), ventral (VS), and tail of striatum (TS).
source: However, M1 injections also labeled a large number of Wt-RABV+ neurons outside the CTb-labeled zone in DLS, including the dorsomedial (DMS), ventral (VS), and tail of striatum (TS) (Figure 1E and F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2I), indicating an open loop in addition to the closed loop.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments shown in the figures.

claim: The finding of Wt-RABV+ neurons in VS, DMS, and TS after M1 injection indicates an open loop in addition to the closed loop.
source: However, M1 injections also labeled a large number of Wt-RABV+ neurons outside the CTb-labeled zone in DLS, including the dorsomedial (DMS), ventral (VS), and tail of striatum (TS) (Figure 1E and F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2I), indicating an open loop in addition to the closed loop.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical tracing data showing outputs without corresponding inputs.

claim: The finding of VS output to M1 is consistent with primate studies.
source: This finding is consistent with the VS output to M1 in primate studies (Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior primate studies.

claim: Striatal subregions associated with emotional and cognitive (VS and DMS) functions, as well as sensory processing (TS), can target M1 via basal ganglia output, despite having no direct inputs from M1.
source: These data suggest that striatal subregions associated with emotional and cognitive (VS and DMS) functions, as well as sensory processing (TS), can target M1 via basal ganglia output, despite having no direct inputs from M1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical tracing data.

claim: A similar pattern of labeling was observed following M2 injections, where VS, DMS and TS can target M2 without receiving its direct inputs.
source: A similar pattern of labeling was observed following M2 injections, where VS, DMS and TS can target M2 without receiving its direct inputs (Figure 1G–1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D and J), confirming an open loop in addition to the closed motor loop.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Wt-RABV/CTb injections into mPFC revealed a closed limbic loop, where CTb+ terminals and Wt-RABV+ neurons, which largely overlapped, were found only in DMS and VS, with no labeling observed in DLS or TS.
source: In marked contrast, Wt-RABV/CTb injections into mPFC (including prelimbic (PrL) and cingulate cortex) revealed a closed limbic loop, where CTb+ terminals and Wt-RABV+ neurons, which largely overlapped, were found only in DMS and VS, with no labeling observed in DLS or TS (Figure 1J–1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E, F and K).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments shown in the figures.

claim: The distributions of Wt-RABV+ cells across five striatal regions were significantly different based on cortical injection site.
source: We quantified the Wt-RABV+ cells across five striatal regions and found that the distributions were significantly different based on cortical injection site (Figure 1M, main effect of interaction, F(8,40) = 8.208, p<0.0001), suggesting a largely closed cortico-basal ganglia loop architecture within both the limbic and motor domains.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the tracing data with statistical testing.

claim: There is a largely closed cortico-basal ganglia loop architecture within both the limbic and motor domains.
source: We quantified the Wt-RABV+ cells across five striatal regions and found that the distributions were significantly different based on cortical injection site (Figure 1M, main effect of interaction, F(8,40) = 8.208, p<0.0001), suggesting a largely closed cortico-basal ganglia loop architecture within both the limbic and motor domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative analysis of the tracing data.

claim: The absence of Wt-RABV+ cells in DLS following mPFC injections indicates that the motor loop does not affect the limbic loop through the direct pathway.
source: However, while the absence of Wt-RABV+ cells in DLS following mPFC injections indicates that the motor loop does not affect the limbic loop through the direct pathway, the limbic loop can influence motor circuits as revealed by the significant presence of VS labeling from M1/M2 injections (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G, t9 = 4.229, p=0.0022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical tracing data.

claim: The limbic loop can influence motor circuits as revealed by the significant presence of VS labeling from M1/M2 injections.
source: However, while the absence of Wt-RABV+ cells in DLS following mPFC injections indicates that the motor loop does not affect the limbic loop through the direct pathway, the limbic loop can influence motor circuits as revealed by the significant presence of VS labeling from M1/M2 injections (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G, t9 = 4.229, p=0.0022).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the tracing data with statistical testing.

claim: Limbic information originating from ventral striatum can influence motor cortex via the basal ganglia direct pathway output.
source: These findings confirm the existence of closed-loops within both limbic and motor domains in the cortico-basal ganglia circuitry, but importantly, they also reveal that limbic information originating from ventral striatum can also influence motor cortex via the basal ganglia direct pathway output (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical tracing data.

claim: M1 projects to DLS almost exclusively.
source: As reported earlier (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Voorn et al., 2004), M1 projects to DLS almost exclusively, whereas mPFC innervates mainly DMS and to a lesser degree VLS and VMS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and confirmed by the current data.

claim: mPFC innervates mainly DMS and to a lesser degree VLS and VMS.
source: As reported earlier (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Voorn et al., 2004), M1 projects to DLS almost exclusively, whereas mPFC innervates mainly DMS and to a lesser degree VLS and VMS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and confirmed by the current data.

claim: There is a significant interaction between mPFC inputs to the striatum and its outputs to the mPFC.
source: A comparison between mPFC inputs to the striatum and its outputs to the mPFC showed a significant interaction (F(4,15) = 8.022, p=0.0011).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the tracing data.

claim: VMS has a mismatch in which it receives a few inputs but has many outputs.
source: In particular, VMS had a mismatch in which it receives a few inputs but has many outputs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting the possibility that VMS provides a common source for the open loop structure (Miyachi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing data analysis.

claim: VMS may provide a common source for the open loop structure.
source: In particular, VMS had a mismatch in which it receives a few inputs but has many outputs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting the possibility that VMS provides a common source for the open loop structure (Miyachi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed input-output mismatch and cited literature.

claim: There is significant interaction between M1 striatal inputs and striatal outputs to the M1.
source: There was also significant interaction between M1 striatal inputs and striatal outputs to the M1 (F(4,20) = 15.5, p<0.0001; Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the tracing data.

claim: Only DLS receives M1 inputs but multiple striatal regions (VMS, VLS, DMS, DLS and TS) connect to M1.
source: This result indicates that only DLS receives M1 inputs but that multiple striatal regions (VMS, VLS, DMS, DLS and TS) connect to M1, implying that all striatal outputs are funneled into M1 via basal ganglia direct pathway output.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing data analysis.

claim: All striatal outputs are funneled into M1 via basal ganglia direct pathway output.
source: This result indicates that only DLS receives M1 inputs but that multiple striatal regions (VMS, VLS, DMS, DLS and TS) connect to M1, implying that all striatal outputs are funneled into M1 via basal ganglia direct pathway output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical tracing data showing convergence of outputs.

claim: The use of AAVretro serotype induced retrograde Cre expression in SNr neurons projecting to VA-VL.
source: Second, the use of the AAVretro serotype induced retrograde Cre expression in SNr neurons projecting to VA-VL (Tervo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to the AAVretro paper.

claim: Analysis of midbrain nuclei revealed mCherry+ cells in SNr, with virtually no co-localization with tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive cells (less than 4%).
source: Analysis of midbrain nuclei revealed mCherry+ cells in SNr, with virtually no co-localization with tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive cells (less than 4%), indicating that only non-dopaminergic SNr neurons project to VA-VL (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: Only non-dopaminergic SNr neurons project to VA-VL.
source: Analysis of midbrain nuclei revealed mCherry+ cells in SNr, with virtually no co-localization with tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive cells (less than 4%), indicating that only non-dopaminergic SNr neurons project to VA-VL (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of TH co-localization in the labeled cells.

claim: Starter cells defined by mCherry+ and Rt-RABV-GFP+ were located throughout the medial to lateral extent of SNr.
source: Starter cells defined by mCherry+ and Rt-RABV-GFP+ (Callaway and Luo, 2015) were located throughout the medial to lateral extent of SNr (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rabies tracing experiments.

claim: Transfection of the monosynaptic rabies virus was observed throughout the striatum, including VS, DMS, DLS and TS.
source: Transfection of the monosynaptic rabies virus was observed throughout the striatum, including VS, DMS, DLS and TS (Figure 2F–2G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rabies tracing experiments.

claim: The monosynaptic rabies tracing result is consistent with the wild-type rabies tracing from M1, and they shared almost identical quantitative distributions.
source: This result is consistent with the wild-type rabies tracing from M1, and they shared almost identical quantitative distributions (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison of the two tracing methods.

claim: All striatal regions, including limbic VS, reach motor cortex through the basal ganglia direct pathway, by the striato-nigro-thalamic route.
source: These findings support our Wt-RABV data demonstrating that all striatal regions, including limbic VS, reach motor cortex through the basal ganglia direct pathway, that is, by the striato-nigro-thalamic route (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined Wt-RABV and Rt-RABV tracing data.

claim: There is an absence of VP neurons labeled after the Wt-RABV injection in M1.
source: Notably, there is an absence of VP neurons labeled after the Wt-RABV injection in M1 or Rt-RABV tracing from VA-VL-projecting SNr neurons (B, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: There is an absence of VP neurons labeled after Rt-RABV tracing from VA-VL-projecting SNr neurons.
source: Notably, there is an absence of VP neurons labeled after the Wt-RABV injection in M1 or Rt-RABV tracing from VA-VL-projecting SNr neurons (B, C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: There was almost no labeling in VP in Rt-RABV tracing from SNr neurons projecting to VA-VL, as opposed to the dense labeling in GPe and STN.
source: There was almost no labeling in VP in Rt-RABV tracing from SNr neurons projecting to VA-VL, as opposed to the dense labeling in GPe and STN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The limbic-to-motor interaction does not occur through the ventral striatum to ventral pallidum pathway.
source: This result suggests that the limbic-to-motor interaction does not occur through the ventral striatum to ventral pallidum pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of VP labeling in the relevant tracing experiments.

claim: Virtually all striatal regions have outputs to motor thalamus.
source: Since virtually all striatal regions have outputs to motor thalamus (Figure 2), it follows that there must be convergence from the entire SNr onto thalamo-cortical neurons projecting to M1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rabies tracing data from Figure 2.

claim: There must be convergence from the entire SNr onto thalamo-cortical neurons projecting to M1.
source: Since virtually all striatal regions have outputs to motor thalamus (Figure 2), it follows that there must be convergence from the entire SNr onto thalamo-cortical neurons projecting to M1.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the anatomical tracing data.

claim: Starter cells defined as both TVA.mCherry+ and Rt-RABV-GFP+ were found in VA-VL.
source: Starter cells defined as both TVA.mCherry+ and Rt-RABV-GFP+ were found in VA-VL, whereas the adjacent thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) showed only Rt-RABV-GFP+ cells (Figure 3B), suggesting that the primary starter cells are located selectively in VA-VL, and that labeling in TRN resulted from trans-synaptic rabies transfection.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rabies tracing experiments.

claim: The adjacent thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) showed only Rt-RABV-GFP+ cells.
source: Starter cells defined as both TVA.mCherry+ and Rt-RABV-GFP+ were found in VA-VL, whereas the adjacent thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) showed only Rt-RABV-GFP+ cells (Figure 3B), suggesting that the primary starter cells are located selectively in VA-VL, and that labeling in TRN resulted from trans-synaptic rabies transfection.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rabies tracing experiments.

claim: The primary starter cells are located selectively in VA-VL, and labeling in TRN resulted from trans-synaptic rabies transfection.
source: Starter cells defined as both TVA.mCherry+ and Rt-RABV-GFP+ were found in VA-VL, whereas the adjacent thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) showed only Rt-RABV-GFP+ cells (Figure 3B), suggesting that the primary starter cells are located selectively in VA-VL, and that labeling in TRN resulted from trans-synaptic rabies transfection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential labeling patterns in VA-VL versus TRN.

claim: Cortico-thalamic GFP+ cells were found exclusively in motor cortex, but not in cingulate or prelimbic cortices.
source: Cortico-thalamic GFP+ cells were found exclusively in motor cortex, but not in cingulate or prelimbic cortices (Figure 3C), and GFP+ cerebello-thalamic cells were located in the dentate and interpositus nuclei (Figure 3D), demonstrating the specificity of our tracing to motor thalamus.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rabies tracing experiments.

claim: GFP+ cerebello-thalamic cells were located in the dentate and interpositus nuclei.
source: Cortico-thalamic GFP+ cells were found exclusively in motor cortex, but not in cingulate or prelimbic cortices (Figure 3C), and GFP+ cerebello-thalamic cells were located in the dentate and interpositus nuclei (Figure 3D), demonstrating the specificity of our tracing to motor thalamus.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rabies tracing experiments.

claim: The labeling patterns in cortex and cerebellar nuclei demonstrate the specificity of the tracing to motor thalamus.
source: Cortico-thalamic GFP+ cells were found exclusively in motor cortex, but not in cingulate or prelimbic cortices (Figure 3C), and GFP+ cerebello-thalamic cells were located in the dentate and interpositus nuclei (Figure 3D), demonstrating the specificity of our tracing to motor thalamus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known connectivity patterns of motor thalamus.

claim: Trans-synaptically labeled Rt-RABV-GFP+ cells were found in both medial and lateral SNr, covering the entire territory of the region.
source: Most importantly, we found trans-synaptically labeled Rt-RABV-GFP+ cells in both medial and lateral SNr, covering the entire territory of the region (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rabies tracing experiments.

claim: There is convergence of limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information from both medial and lateral SNr onto thalamo-M1 cells.
source: These findings provide strong evidence for the convergence of limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information from both medial and lateral SNr onto thalamo-M1 cells, and suggest that all basal ganglia outputs provide some amount of convergence into a 'funnel' towards the motor cortex (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rabies tracing data showing widespread SNr inputs to motor thalamus.

claim: All basal ganglia outputs provide some amount of convergence into a 'funnel' towards the motor cortex.
source: These findings provide strong evidence for the convergence of limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information from both medial and lateral SNr onto thalamo-M1 cells, and suggest that all basal ganglia outputs provide some amount of convergence into a 'funnel' towards the motor cortex (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rabies tracing data showing widespread SNr inputs to motor thalamus.

claim: DLS, DMS and VS terminated in different SNr subregions, with VS specifically innervating the most medial region of SNr.
source: Importantly, DLS, DMS and VS terminated in different SNr subregions, with VS specifically innervating the most medial region of SNr (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: Limbic and motor information remain largely segregated at the level of SNr.
source: These data suggest that limbic and motor information remain largely segregated at this stage of basal ganglia output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the segregated terminal fields in SNr.

claim: DS and VS innervate EPN and LH, respectively.
source: In addition, DMS and DLS were found to project topographically to the EPN (Figure 4C and F), whereas VS innervates the adjacent lateral hypothalamus (LH) (Figure 4C), indicating that this alternative direct pathway output nucleus, EPN, is not how limbic information reaches motor cortex.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: EPN is not how limbic information reaches motor cortex.
source: In addition, DMS and DLS were found to project topographically to the EPN (Figure 4C and F), whereas VS innervates the adjacent lateral hypothalamus (LH) (Figure 4C), indicating that this alternative direct pathway output nucleus, EPN, is not how limbic information reaches motor cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of VS projections to EPN.

claim: Lateral SNr, which receives input from DLS, projects to VA-VL and the dorsal part of caudal VM.
source: More careful analysis revealed that lateral SNr, which receives input from DLS, projects to VA-VL and the dorsal part of caudal VM.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: Medial SNr, which receives limbic input from VS, has more diffuse projections and targets MD, VA, rostral VM, and the ventral part of caudal VM.
source: By contrast, medial SNr, which receives limbic input from VS, has more diffuse projections and targets MD, VA, rostral VM, and the ventral part of caudal VM.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: M1- and M2-projecting neurons were found in VA-VL and caudal VM.
source: M1- and M2-projecting neurons were found in VA-VL and caudal VM, whereas mPFC-projecting thalamic neurons were selective to rostral VM and MD (Figure 4J–4L), consistent with previous reports (Collins et al., 2018; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Kuramoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: mPFC-projecting thalamic neurons were selective to rostral VM and MD.
source: M1- and M2-projecting neurons were found in VA-VL and caudal VM, whereas mPFC-projecting thalamic neurons were selective to rostral VM and MD (Figure 4J–4L), consistent with previous reports (Collins et al., 2018; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Kuramoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the retrograde tracing experiments, consistent with prior literature.

claim: Medial SNr projects preferentially to mPFC-projecting 'limbic' thalamus (rostral VM and MD), but also targets M1- and M2-projecting VA and caudal VM 'motor' thalamus.
source: In conjunction with the projection patterns from medial SNr, these data suggest that medial SNr projects preferentially to mPFC-projecting 'limbic' thalamus (rostral VM and MD), but also targets M1- and M2-projecting VA and caudal VM 'motor' thalamus (Figure 4H and I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H), consistent with identified synaptic inputs from medial SNr to thalamo-M1 cells (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anterograde and retrograde tracing data.

claim: A critical node at which limbic output splits into motor circuits is formed by the medial SNr projections to motor thalamus.
source: Therefore, a critical node at which limbic output splits into motor circuits is formed by the medial SNr projections to these regions of motor thalamus (Figure 4M and N), through which the limbic loop can exert its unidirectional influence over the motor loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical tracing data.

claim: The lateral SNr does not project to mPFC-projecting thalamic nuclei.
source: Conversely, the lateral SNr does not project to mPFC-projecting thalamic nuclei (Figure 4G–4L), consistent with the lack of DLS connections to mPFC and suggesting no motor-to-limbic interactions through the direct pathway (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: There are no motor-to-limbic interactions through the direct pathway.
source: Conversely, the lateral SNr does not project to mPFC-projecting thalamic nuclei (Figure 4G–4L), consistent with the lack of DLS connections to mPFC and suggesting no motor-to-limbic interactions through the direct pathway (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of lateral SNr projections to limbic thalamus and the lack of DLS connections to mPFC.

claim: Optogenetic activation of DLS terminals in SNr evoked inhibitory post-synaptic currents (IPSCs) in retrobeads+ neurons in lateral SNr.
source: In brain slices, optogenetic activation of DLS terminals in SNr evoked inhibitory post-synaptic currents (IPSCs) in retrobeads+ neurons in lateral SNr, confirming that DLS functionally synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr neurons (Figure 4O).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the ex vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: DLS functionally synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr neurons.
source: In brain slices, optogenetic activation of DLS terminals in SNr evoked inhibitory post-synaptic currents (IPSCs) in retrobeads+ neurons in lateral SNr, confirming that DLS functionally synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr neurons (Figure 4O).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ex vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Optogenetic activation of VS terminals in SNr evoked IPSCs in retrobeads+ neurons in medial SNr.
source: Notably, optogenetic activation of VS terminals in SNr also evoked IPCSs in retrobeads+ neurons in medial SNr (Figure 4P), confirming that projections from VS to SNr are functional.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the ex vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Projections from VS to SNr are functional.
source: Notably, optogenetic activation of VS terminals in SNr also evoked IPCSs in retrobeads+ neurons in medial SNr (Figure 4P), confirming that projections from VS to SNr are functional.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ex vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: There is no significant difference in the IPSC amplitude between VS- and DLS-synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr cells.
source: Comparison of both the IPSC amplitude (Figure 4Q) and the paired-pulse ratio (Figure 4R) revealed no significant difference in the strength or general properties between VS- and DLS-synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr cells, suggesting that both VS and DLS can equally modulate SNr activity.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the electrophysiology data.

claim: There is no significant difference in the paired-pulse ratio between VS- and DLS-synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr cells.
source: Comparison of both the IPSC amplitude (Figure 4Q) and the paired-pulse ratio (Figure 4R) revealed no significant difference in the strength or general properties between VS- and DLS-synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr cells, suggesting that both VS and DLS can equally modulate SNr activity.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the electrophysiology data.

claim: Both VS and DLS can equally modulate SNr activity.
source: Comparison of both the IPSC amplitude (Figure 4Q) and the paired-pulse ratio (Figure 4R) revealed no significant difference in the strength or general properties between VS- and DLS-synapses onto motor thalamus-projecting SNr cells, suggesting that both VS and DLS can equally modulate SNr activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant differences in synaptic properties.

claim: Inputs to medial and lateral SNr come from segregated populations in VS/DMS, and DLS, respectively.
source: Both anterograde and retrograde tracing of striato-nigral projections confirmed that inputs to medial and lateral SNr come from segregated populations in VS/DMS, and DLS, respectively (Figure 4A–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), allowing us to target their outputs individually using optogenetics.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments.

claim: 24% of neurons recorded in M1 were responsive to the activation of DLS terminals in SNr.
source: We found that 24% (44/189 recorded cells) of neurons recorded in M1 were responsive to the activation of DLS terminals in SNr (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The activation of the striatal direct pathway mostly increased cortical neuron firing rates.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Lee et al., 2016; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015), the activation of the striatal direct pathway mostly increased cortical neuron firing rates (Figure 5E and G), rather than inhibiting the firing of these neurons (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vivo electrophysiology experiments, consistent with prior literature.

claim: 12% of M1 neurons responded to VS terminal activation.
source: Strikingly, 12% (18/154) of M1 neurons also responded to VS terminal activation, demonstrating that VS output alters the activity of M1 in vivo (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: VS output alters the activity of M1 in vivo.
source: Strikingly, 12% (18/154) of M1 neurons also responded to VS terminal activation, demonstrating that VS output alters the activity of M1 in vivo (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: mPFC neurons responded selectively to the stimulation of VS terminals in medial SNr (35%, 56/158), but not to DLS terminal stimulation (3%, 4/159).
source: Conversely, mPFC neurons responded selectively to the stimulation of VS terminals in medial SNr (35%, 56/158), but not to DLS terminal stimulation (3%, 4/159) (Figure 5L–S).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: A significantly greater portion of M1 neurons respond to VS stimulation than of mPFC neurons that are responsive to DLS stimulation.
source: Comparison of the proportion of neurons that changed their activity in response to optical stimulation indicated a significantly greater portion of M1 neurons responding to VS stimulation than of mPFC neurons that were responsive to DLS stimulation (Figure 5T, p=0.0015).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of the in vivo electrophysiology data.

claim: 8% of M1 neurons responded to the VS activation with a latency of 5–35 ms when activating D1R neurons in VS.
source: Moreover, we tested the effect of activation of the VS direct pathway neurons (D1R neurons) on M1 activity using D1-Cre mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2P–T). This indicated that 8% of M1 neurons responded to the VS activation with a latency of 5–35 ms, further supporting the results of our terminal stimulation experiments.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the in vivo electrophysiology experiments using D1-Cre mice.

claim: There is a one-way influence of limbic loops onto motor loops.
source: In this study, we dissected the topography of limbic and motor cortico-basal ganglia loops at each synaptic step and revealed a one-way influence of limbic loops onto motor loops.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: The data demonstrate mostly closed cortico-basal ganglia loops within each domain.
source: Although our data do demonstrate mostly closed cortico-basal ganglia loops within each domain, our results confirm an open cortico-basal ganglia loop that allows for a one-way interaction from limbic to motor circuitry (Figure 5U).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical tracing data.

claim: The results confirm an open cortico-basal ganglia loop that allows for a one-way interaction from limbic to motor circuitry.
source: Although our data do demonstrate mostly closed cortico-basal ganglia loops within each domain, our results confirm an open cortico-basal ganglia loop that allows for a one-way interaction from limbic to motor circuitry (Figure 5U).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: The open-loop structure revealed is consistent with earlier studies in primates that have identified multi-synaptic connectivity from ventral putamen to M1.
source: The open-loop structure that we revealed here is consistent with earlier studies in primates that have identified multi-synaptic connectivity from ventral putamen to M1 (Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006), with conceptual work on the convergence of basal ganglia outputs to motor circuits (Allen and Tsukahara, 1974; Haber, 2003; Joel and Weiner, 1994; Kemp and Powell, 1971), and with behavioral findings that suggest the involvement of VS in modifying motor output (Belin and Everitt, 2008; Floresco, 2015; Sawada et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The findings are consistent with conceptual work on the convergence of basal ganglia outputs to motor circuits.
source: The open-loop structure that we revealed here is consistent with earlier studies in primates that have identified multi-synaptic connectivity from ventral putamen to M1 (Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006), with conceptual work on the convergence of basal ganglia outputs to motor circuits (Allen and Tsukahara, 1974; Haber, 2003; Joel and Weiner, 1994; Kemp and Powell, 1971), and with behavioral findings that suggest the involvement of VS in modifying motor output (Belin and Everitt, 2008; Floresco, 2015; Sawada et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The findings are consistent with behavioral findings that suggest the involvement of VS in modifying motor output.
source: The open-loop structure that we revealed here is consistent with earlier studies in primates that have identified multi-synaptic connectivity from ventral putamen to M1 (Kelly and Strick, 2004; Miyachi et al., 2006), with conceptual work on the convergence of basal ganglia outputs to motor circuits (Allen and Tsukahara, 1974; Haber, 2003; Joel and Weiner, 1994; Kemp and Powell, 1971), and with behavioral findings that suggest the involvement of VS in modifying motor output (Belin and Everitt, 2008; Floresco, 2015; Sawada et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The study confirmed limbic-to-motor connectivity by trans-synaptic rabies tracing.
source: In the present study, we confirmed this limbic-to-motor connectivity by trans-synaptic rabies tracing, two distinct circuit-specific monosynaptic rabies tracing experiments (nigro-thalamic and thalamo-cortical), and viral tracing combined with transgenic mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological approaches used in the study.

claim: The study demonstrated functionality of the limbic-to-motor pathway by ex vivo slice recordings.
source: Subsequently, we demonstrated its functionality by ex vivo slice recordings, which physiologically showed inhibition of motor-thalamus projecting SNr neurons by VS inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of the ex vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: In vivo electrophysiology recordings verified functional closed loops within VS-mPFC and DLS-M1.
source: We further carried out in vivo electrophysiology recordings that verified functional closed loops within VS-mPFC and DLS-M1, and that also found significant activation of M1 by VS inputs to SNr, in contrast to the absence of modulation of mPFC by the DLS inputs to SNr.
evidence: This is a summary of the in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: In vivo electrophysiology found significant activation of M1 by VS inputs to SNr.
source: We further carried out in vivo electrophysiology recordings that verified functional closed loops within VS-mPFC and DLS-M1, and that also found significant activation of M1 by VS inputs to SNr, in contrast to the absence of modulation of mPFC by the DLS inputs to SNr.
evidence: This is a summary of the in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: In vivo electrophysiology found an absence of modulation of mPFC by the DLS inputs to SNr.
source: We further carried out in vivo electrophysiology recordings that verified functional closed loops within VS-mPFC and DLS-M1, and that also found significant activation of M1 by VS inputs to SNr, in contrast to the absence of modulation of mPFC by the DLS inputs to SNr.
evidence: This is a summary of the in vivo electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The findings suggest considerable functional influence of limbic striatal output on M1 activity.
source: These findings suggest considerable functional influence of limbic striatal output on M1 activity and reveal a more complex framework of interactions across functionally distinct cortico-basal ganglia loops than is widely appreciated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: The findings reveal a more complex framework of interactions across functionally distinct cortico-basal ganglia loops than is widely appreciated.
source: These findings suggest considerable functional influence of limbic striatal output on M1 activity and reveal a more complex framework of interactions across functionally distinct cortico-basal ganglia loops than is widely appreciated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: DMS and TS were also found to connect to the motor cortex.
source: In addition to VS, the other striatal territories, including DMS and TS, were also found to connect to the motor cortex, suggesting a wider theme of all modalities converging onto motor circuits, in addition to their within-domain interactions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tracing experiments.

claim: All modalities converge onto motor circuits, in addition to their within-domain interactions.
source: In addition to VS, the other striatal territories, including DMS and TS, were also found to connect to the motor cortex, suggesting a wider theme of all modalities converging onto motor circuits, in addition to their within-domain interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical tracing data showing multiple striatal regions connecting to motor cortex.

claim: Striatal outputs throughout basal ganglia are motor-oriented in nature while maintaining domain-dependent closed loops.
source: Unlike the topographically segregated cortico-striatal projections, we propose that striatal outputs throughout basal ganglia are motor-oriented in nature while maintaining domain-dependent closed loops, likely structured to be able to drive behavioral output in various contexts determined by the inputs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined anatomical data.

claim: VS has been suggested to be involved in Pavlovian approach.
source: For instance, VS has been suggested to be involved in Pavlovian approach (Saunders and Robinson, 2012) and in emotion-driven actions such as avoidance behavior (Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VS has been suggested to be involved in emotion-driven actions such as avoidance behavior.
source: For instance, VS has been suggested to be involved in Pavlovian approach (Saunders and Robinson, 2012) and in emotion-driven actions such as avoidance behavior (Ramirez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A recent study in primates found that VS plays a crucial role in the recovery of skilled movement after spinal cord injury, by driving neural activity in primary motor cortex.
source: Notably, a recent study in primates has found that VS plays a crucial role in the recovery of skilled movement after spinal cord injury, by driving neural activity in primary motor cortex (Sawada et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior primate study.

claim: The results offer a mechanism through which limbic information originating from ventral striatum can influence motor cortex and motor output via the nigro-thalamic pathway.
source: Our results offer a mechanism through which limbic information originating from ventral striatum can influence motor cortex and motor output via the nigro-thalamic pathway, providing an anatomical foundation that is capable of supporting these behavioral changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: A unidirectional limbic-to-motor influence through this pathway implies that selecting and invigorating action can be determined by emotional and motivational states.
source: Overall, a unidirectional limbic-to-motor influence through this pathway implies that selecting and invigorating action can be determined by emotional and motivational states.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications of the anatomical findings.

claim: The DMS receives cognitive information from higher-order association cortex.
source: The DMS receives cognitive information from higher-order association cortex and is known to be crucial for internally driven, goal-directed behavior (Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The DMS is known to be crucial for internally driven, goal-directed behavior.
source: The DMS receives cognitive information from higher-order association cortex and is known to be crucial for internally driven, goal-directed behavior (Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TS has been thought to primarily process various modalities of sensory information from the external world.
source: On the other hand, TS has been thought to primarily process various modalities of sensory information from the external world (Alloway et al., 2017; Hintiryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests that TS is involved in responses to novel or salient stimuli.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that TS is involved in responses to novel or salient stimuli (Menegas et al., 2018) and in sensory-guided action selection (Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: TS is involved in sensory-guided action selection.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that TS is involved in responses to novel or salient stimuli (Menegas et al., 2018) and in sensory-guided action selection (Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The study uncovered a mechanism through which the DMS and TS can interact with motor cortex, enabling information involving internal and external states to affect motor circuits for guiding motor output.
source: In the present study, we uncovered a mechanism through which the DMS and TS can interact with motor cortex, enabling information involving internal and external states to affect motor circuits for guiding motor output.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical tracing data showing DMS and TS connections to motor cortex.

claim: It has been known that single SNr neurons have dendrites that extend broadly across the medio-lateral extent of SNr.
source: It is plausible that the limbic and motor integration occurs as early as SNr, as it has been known that single SNr neurons have dendrites that extend broadly across the medio-lateral extent of SNr (Mailly et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Prior studies showed that SNr neurons receive functionally distinct inputs from striatum and other indirect pathway nuclei.
source: In fact, prior studies showed that SNr neurons receive functionally distinct inputs from striatum and other indirect pathway nuclei (Bevan et al., 1994; Bevan et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous studies have identified direct projections from external globus pallidus (GPe) and subthalamic nucleus (STN) to the frontal cortex.
source: In addition to the classical basal ganglia direct pathway output to cortex, previous studies have identified direct projections from external globus pallidus (GPe) and subthalamic nucleus (STN) to the frontal cortex (Chen et al., 2015; Jackson and Crossman, 1981; Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Interactions across cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops are also enabled by dopamine modulation with the divergent projections from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) targeting both dorsal and ventral striatum.
source: In addition, interactions across cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops are also enabled by dopamine modulation with the divergent projections from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) targeting both dorsal and ventral striatum (Beier et al., 2015; Haber et al., 2000; Lerner et al., 2015; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The findings have important implications in a wide range of neurological and psychiatric diseases, from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) to anxiety and depression, in which the limbic control of action is compromised.
source: These findings pave the way for a more complete understanding of fundamental aspects of behaviors such as action sequencing and habit formation (Dickinson, 1985; Jin and Costa, 2015; Yin and Knowlton, 2006), and have important implications in a wide range of neurological and psychiatric diseases, from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) to anxiety and depression, in which the limbic control of action is compromised (Everitt and Robbins, 2005; Marchand et al., 2012; Redgrave et al., 2010; Robbins et al., 2012; Vaghi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about the clinical implications of the findings, supported by citations to prior literature.
